about.title: Mammoth Lakes Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Mammoth Lakes sees heavy seasonal foot traffic from skiers, hikers, and visitors moving between lodges, restaurants, and shops along Main Street, Minaret Road, and Old Mammoth Road. That mix of snow, ice, and uneven mountain-town walkways creates real fall hazards property owners are supposed to manage. Under California law, a property owner or business generally has to have known — or reasonably should have known — about a dangerous condition before they can be held responsible for not fixing or warning about it. That's why documenting what actually caused your fall matters so much: photos of ice buildup, a torn mat, poor lighting, or a broken step can make the difference in a claim. Surveillance footage at hotels, condos, and retail spaces often gets overwritten within days or weeks, so acting quickly to preserve it is important. LawProactive doesn't practice law itself, but we can connect you with an independent attorney who understands how these claims work in a resort town like Mammoth Lakes.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a Mammoth Lakes Premises Case

items.title: Proving the Owner Knew or Should Have Known
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner had notice of the hazard, whether that's an ice patch that sat unaddressed or a broken step reported before. An attorney can help gather maintenance logs, prior complaints, or weather records to build that picture.

items.title: Preserving Surveillance Before It's Gone
items.desc: Hotels, condos, and shops around Main Street and Minaret Road often overwrite security footage within days. Getting a preservation request out quickly can be the difference between having proof and having none.

items.title: Accounting for Comparative Fault
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, meaning your recovery can be reduced by your share of blame but isn't automatically barred. An attorney can help push back on unfair fault arguments, especially in icy or seasonal conditions.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Mammoth Lakes?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit against a private property owner. If the fall happened on public property, like a town-owned walkway or building, the deadline is much shorter and involves an early claim filing. It's worth having an attorney check the specifics of your situation soon after the fall.

items.question: Does Mammoth Lakes' snow and ice affect who's responsible for a fall?
items.answer: Snow and ice don't automatically make a property owner liable — the question is still whether they knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to reasonably address it, like clearing walkways or salting entrances. Given how much of Mammoth Lakes' foot traffic happens in winter conditions, this notice requirement often becomes the central issue in a claim.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for my own fall?
items.answer: California's pure comparative fault rule means you can still recover damages even if you were partly responsible, though the amount may be reduced by your percentage of fault. This comes up often in fall cases, so having documentation of the hazard itself helps counter arguments that you weren't paying attention.
